basic_information.name: AI Business Canvas / Lean AI
basic_information.description: A family of adapted business model frameworks designed specifically for AI ventures, encompassing multiple complementary canvases: (1) the Agrawal-Gans-Goldfarb AI Canvas (HBR 2018) for AI-augmented decision-making with 7 components (prediction, judgment, action, outcome, input, training, feedback); (2) the Kevin Dewalt AI Canvas for enterprise ML feasibility (business left, technical right); (3) the Louis Dorard Machine Learning Canvas (10 blocks from value proposition to live evaluation); (4) the Kerzel Enterprise AI Canvas (2020) bridging data scientists and business experts; (5) the Lomit Patel Lean AI methodology extending Eric Ries's Lean Startup with AI-powered growth loops; and (6) the emerging 'Rethinking Lean Startup for AI' movement that adds LLM behavior observation to the Build-Measure-Learn cycle. Together these frameworks help AI founders and enterprise teams plan, validate, and scale AI-powered products and business models.
source_companies: OpenAI (exemplar AI business model, $13B ARR by Aug 2025)
Anthropic (enterprise AI leader, 40% enterprise LLM spend 2025)
Midjourney (super lean AI startup, ~11 employees, high revenue/employee)
OWNML (Louis Dorard's Machine Learning Canvas platform)
Prediction Machines / Creative Destruction Lab (Agrawal, Gans, Goldfarb)
basic_information.time_period: 2018-2026 (original canvases from 2017-2020, Lean AI book 2020, active evolution through 2025-2026 with generative AI adaptations)

business_model_structure.revenue_model: The frameworks themselves are primarily disseminated through books, consulting, and SaaS tools. Strategyzer monetizes via SaaS platform subscriptions ($8.3M revenue, 75-person team). Lomit Patel's Lean AI is monetized through O'Reilly book sales and consulting. The canvases are largely open frameworks (free templates, academic papers) but generate revenue through adjacent consulting, training programs, and enterprise software. Companies using these frameworks adopt revenue models ranging from subscription and usage-based pricing to outcome-based and hybrid models depending on their AI product type.
business_model_structure.pricing_strategy: Strategyzer: tiered SaaS pricing for canvas tools. OWNML Machine Learning Canvas: free template + paid workshops and training. The frameworks themselves recommend AI startups consider per-token pricing, per-outcome pricing, freemium with AI-powered tiers, or credit-based models. The Lean AI methodology specifically advocates starting with freemium to validate product-market fit, then layering premium AI features. Enterprise AI Canvas tools typically use per-seat enterprise licensing.
business_model_structure.cost_structure: For the framework providers: primarily talent (content creators, consultants, developers), platform hosting, and marketing. For companies applying these frameworks to build AI businesses: compute costs represent 20-50% of COGS for inference-heavy products, data acquisition and labeling costs, AI talent (ML engineers commanding $200-400K+ salaries), and distribution/go-to-market. The Lean AI approach specifically aims to minimize costs by using AI automation before hiring humans — super lean AI startups average just 22-24 employees generating $2.5-3.5M revenue per employee.
business_model_structure.value_proposition: Provide structured, repeatable frameworks for planning, validating, and scaling AI ventures. The Agrawal AI Canvas demystifies AI decision-making for non-technical executives. The Dewalt AI Canvas bridges business and technical feasibility for enterprise ML projects. The Dorard ML Canvas provides data science teams with systematic project planning. The Enterprise AI Canvas facilitates cross-functional collaboration between data scientists and business experts. The Lean AI methodology accelerates the Build-Measure-Learn loop using AI automation, enabling startups to test, learn, and iterate radically faster.
business_model_structure.target_customer: AI startup founders, enterprise innovation teams, business school students, product managers building AI products, corporate strategy teams evaluating AI opportunities, venture capitalists assessing AI investments, data science teams planning ML projects
business_model_structure.distribution_channel: Books (O'Reilly for Lean AI, HBR Press for Prediction Machines), academic publications (HBR articles, arXiv papers), SaaS platforms (Strategyzer, OWNML, Miro, Creately), Medium/blog posts, consulting engagements, university courses and MBA programs, conference workshops, free downloadable PDF templates
business_model_structure.monetization_timeline: The frameworks are largely free or low-cost to access (academic papers, blog posts, free templates). Monetization happens through: (1) book sales — immediate but modest; (2) SaaS tools — 12-24 months to meaningful ARR; (3) consulting and training — immediate per-engagement revenue; (4) for companies applying these frameworks, the Lean AI approach targets MVP validation within weeks using AI, with meaningful revenue potential within 6-12 months due to accelerated iteration cycles.

financial_metrics.revenue_range: Strategyzer (BMC tool provider): $8.3M revenue in 2025. The broader strategic planning and consulting tools market that these frameworks serve was valued at $49.5B in 2025, projected to reach $107.9B by 2035. For companies applying Lean AI methodology: super lean AI startups generate average $3.48M revenue per employee. Top examples include Midjourney (~$200M+ revenue, ~11 employees) and companies like Bolt reaching $200M ARR.
financial_metrics.gross_margin: For framework/tool providers like Strategyzer: estimated 70-85% gross margins (SaaS model with low compute needs). For AI companies using these frameworks: gross margins vary widely — AI SaaS companies typically achieve 60-75% gross margins, but compute-intensive inference services may see 40-60% margins. The key driver is compute cost optimization: using fine-tuned smaller models (e.g., 7B parameter) can be 10x cheaper than frontier model APIs.
financial_metrics.burn_rate: Not directly applicable to the frameworks themselves. For AI startups applying Lean AI principles: the methodology specifically targets minimal burn by using AI before hiring humans. Super lean AI startups average 22-24 employees, dramatically reducing burn compared to traditional startups. The Lean AI approach aims for capital-efficient growth, though some AI infrastructure companies still require significant upfront investment ($5-50M+ for model training).
financial_metrics.cac_ltv_ratio: Not directly measured for frameworks. For companies using these frameworks: the AI Canvas and Lean AI approaches both emphasize optimizing CAC/LTV — the Lean AI Growth Loop specifically uses AI-powered lead scoring and customer segmentation to reduce CAC. AI-native startups using these frameworks report 3-5x improvements in CAC efficiency through AI-driven marketing automation and product-led growth.
financial_metrics.funding_total: Strategyzer: bootstrapped to $8.3M revenue. The AI companies exemplifying these frameworks have raised massive rounds — OpenAI: $17.9B+ total funding, Anthropic: $13B Series F (2025), with AI funding accounting for ~50-53% of all VC investment in late 2025 (~$190-200B total AI venture funding). Lean AI startups often raise less: $10-50M is typical for capital-efficient AI-first companies.
financial_metrics.valuation: Strategyzer: private, estimated $50-80M range based on SaaS multiples [uncertain]. AI companies applying these frameworks span enormous range — Anthropic valued at $183B post-money (2025), OpenAI at $300B+ (2025). Super lean AI startups that successfully apply Lean AI principles often achieve outsized valuations relative to team size due to high revenue per employee metrics.
financial_metrics.arr_growth_rate: Strategyzer: not publicly disclosed. The AI sector applying these frameworks shows explosive growth — OpenAI grew from $1B to $13B ARR in roughly 18 months (2024-2025), Anthropic grew from ~$100M to $3B+ ARR in 2 years. AI SaaS tools market growing at 25-40% CAGR.
financial_metrics.path_to_profitability: Framework providers like Strategyzer appear operationally profitable (75-person team, $8.3M revenue). For AI companies using these frameworks: the Lean AI approach explicitly targets faster profitability through minimal team sizes and AI automation. Super lean AI startups can reach profitability with fewer than 25 employees. However, foundation model companies (OpenAI, Anthropic) remain unprofitable due to massive compute and research spending. The frameworks help non-foundation-model AI startups plan realistic paths to profitability.

market_positioning.competitive_landscape: Multiple competing and complementary frameworks: (1) Agrawal AI Canvas (HBR, academic credibility, decision-focused); (2) Dewalt AI Canvas (enterprise ML feasibility, practitioner-oriented); (3) Dorard ML Canvas (technical ML project planning, data science teams); (4) Kerzel Enterprise AI Canvas (academic, cross-functional bridge); (5) Osterwalder/Strategyzer BMC (original canvas, now AI-enhanced); (6) Lean Canvas by Ash Maurya (startup-focused, problem-solution oriented); (7) Lomit Patel Lean AI (growth-focused, AI automation). Competitive dynamics: Strategyzer dominates the general canvas market but lacks AI-specific depth. The AI-specific canvases compete on technical depth vs. accessibility. Lean AI competes with traditional Lean Startup and Y Combinator's startup playbook.
market_positioning.market_size_tam: Business model innovation and strategic planning tools market: $49.5B in 2025 (strategy consulting market per Technavio). AI-specific strategic planning tools represent a smaller but rapidly growing segment. The broader AI market that these frameworks serve to plan for: estimated $2.5T+ by 2026 (Gartner). AI startup advisory and consulting specifically: estimated $5-10B segment [uncertain].
market_positioning.differentiation: Each canvas differentiates on a different axis: Agrawal AI Canvas — simplest, most accessible for non-technical executives (7 factors in two rows); Dewalt AI Canvas — balances business and technical feasibility for enterprise ML; Dorard ML Canvas — most technical depth for data science teams (10 blocks); Enterprise AI Canvas — best for cross-functional enterprise collaboration; Lean AI — uniquely focuses on growth and scaling rather than just planning; Rethinking Lean Startup for AI — newest, addresses LLM/generative AI specifically with error analysis and model behavior observation. The collective differentiation from generic business tools is AI-specific blocks: data strategy, model dependency, compute costs, prediction quality, training data requirements.
market_positioning.moat_type: For framework creators: brand and intellectual property (Osterwalder's BMC is the canonical business model tool, Agrawal's 'Prediction Machines' brand). Network effects for SaaS tools (more users = better templates, benchmarks). For companies using these frameworks: the frameworks help identify and build moats including data moats, workflow lock-in, and vertical specialization. A16z identifies proprietary data as the key AI moat — becoming the 'system of record' where accumulated private result data cannot be obtained by general models.
market_positioning.market_share: Strategyzer dominates the general BMC market with millions of users. In AI-specific canvases, no single framework dominates — Agrawal's AI Canvas has the highest academic citation count and HBR visibility, while Dorard's ML Canvas has the most practitioner adoption among data science teams. Lean AI has strong recognition in startup/growth circles through the O'Reilly Lean series. Market is fragmented with room for consolidation. [uncertain]

ai_specific_economics.compute_cost_ratio: These frameworks explicitly help plan for compute costs. Typical AI startups using these frameworks allocate 20-50% of COGS to compute/inference. The Enterprise AI Canvas and Dewalt AI Canvas include dedicated blocks for infrastructure and compute planning. Key insight from Lean AI: using fine-tuned 7B parameter models for specific tasks can be 10x cheaper and 2x faster than generic frontier model APIs, dramatically improving unit economics. Super lean AI startups optimize compute through model distillation and efficient inference.
ai_specific_economics.data_advantage: Data strategy is a central component across all AI canvases. The Dewalt AI Canvas explicitly states 'unique data assets provide the only ongoing sustainable advantage in AI products.' The Agrawal AI Canvas frames data through input data (for predictions) and training data (for model improvement). The Dorard ML Canvas dedicates multiple blocks to data sources, collecting data, and features. Greylock's 'New New Moats' thesis: systems of intelligence that cross multiple datasets create durable moats. A16z: proprietary result data from customer interactions is the new walled garden.
ai_specific_economics.model_dependency: The frameworks help assess and manage model dependency. The Dewalt AI Canvas includes a 'Transfer Learning' block for evaluating foundation model dependencies. The Rethinking Lean Startup for AI approach explicitly addresses model version dependency — product experience depends on model outputs that vary by prompt, context, and model version. Key risk: dependency on specific foundation models (OpenAI, Anthropic APIs) creates vendor lock-in. The frameworks recommend multi-model strategies and fine-tuned open-source alternatives to reduce dependency.
ai_specific_economics.api_cost_structure: The AI canvases help plan API cost structures. Typical patterns: AI wrapper companies absorb 30-60% of revenue as API/inference costs to foundation model providers. Companies using the Lean AI approach aim to reduce this through fine-tuning and model distillation. The Enterprise AI Canvas includes cost modeling for both training and inference. API cost trends: inference costs have dropped 10-100x from 2023 to 2025 across major providers, but volume growth often offsets per-unit savings.
ai_specific_economics.inference_cost_trend: Inference costs are declining rapidly — roughly 10-100x reduction from 2023-2025 across major model providers. This trend is central to AI business planning: the frameworks help entrepreneurs model scenarios where falling inference costs improve unit economics over time. The DeepSeek disruption in early 2025 demonstrated that comparable quality can be achieved at dramatically lower inference costs. The Lean AI methodology specifically plans for this: start with API-based inference, migrate to fine-tuned smaller models as scale justifies the investment.
ai_specific_economics.training_cost_economics: Training costs addressed primarily by the Enterprise AI Canvas and ML Canvas frameworks. Training GPT-4 reportedly cost $100M+, while fine-tuning smaller models for specific tasks costs $1K-$100K. The frameworks help distinguish between companies that need to train foundation models (massive CapEx, few can afford) vs. fine-tune existing models (accessible for startups) vs. use prompt engineering only (lowest cost, highest model dependency). The Lean AI approach favors starting with zero training costs (API usage) and investing in fine-tuning only after product-market fit is validated.
ai_specific_economics.energy_cost_factor: Emerging consideration in AI canvases as of 2025-2026. Data center energy consumption is becoming a significant business model input. European startups face higher energy costs than US counterparts. The EU AI Act's sustainability reporting requirements add compliance costs. The frameworks increasingly include energy/sustainability blocks or considerations, though this was not a primary focus of the original 2018-2020 canvas designs.

scaling_and_growth.growth_strategy: The Lean AI methodology provides the most explicit growth framework among these canvases: (1) Lean AI Growth Loop — Identify & Prioritize → Hypothesize → Test → Measure → Learn → Iterate, applying AI to each step; (2) Customer-Centric AI Blueprint — using AI for personalized customer acquisition and retention; (3) Operational Efficiency Engine — AI automation replacing manual processes. Additional frameworks: Product-Led Growth (PLG) is the dominant strategy for AI tools, where the AI capability itself drives adoption. Enterprise sales for complex AI Canvas implementations. Community-driven growth through open-source frameworks and free canvas templates.
scaling_and_growth.network_effects: The AI canvases help identify and plan network effects: (1) Data network effects — more users generate more data, improving model quality (central to Dewalt and Dorard canvases); (2) Marketplace network effects — AI marketplaces where more sellers attract more buyers; (3) Community network effects — open-source AI tools where community contributions improve the product. Greylock's 'New New Moats': systems of intelligence that combine web analytics, customer data, and social data create network effects through cross-dataset intelligence. A16z: proprietary result data accumulates as companies handle more cases, creating a data flywheel competitors cannot replicate.
scaling_and_growth.flywheel_description: The AI Business Canvas/Lean AI flywheel operates on multiple levels: (1) Framework adoption flywheel — more practitioners use the canvas → more case studies and templates → more credibility → more adoption; (2) AI product flywheel (what the frameworks help design) — more users → more data → better models → better product → more users; (3) Lean AI Growth Loop flywheel — faster experimentation → faster learning → better product decisions → faster growth → more resources for experimentation. The super lean AI startup flywheel specifically: AI automation → fewer employees needed → lower costs → higher margins → reinvest in AI capabilities → more automation.
scaling_and_growth.scalability_model: Improving with scale. The frameworks are designed to help companies plan for improving unit economics: (1) AI inference costs decrease with scale (volume discounts, custom silicon optimization); (2) Data advantages compound — the Enterprise AI Canvas explicitly plans for data accumulation improving model quality; (3) The Lean AI approach targets near-zero marginal cost at scale through AI automation; (4) Revenue per employee for super lean AI startups ($3.48M average) dramatically exceeds traditional SaaS ($610K average), indicating 5.7x better scalability. However, some AI business models face degrading economics at extreme scale due to compute costs growing with usage.
scaling_and_growth.geographic_expansion: The frameworks have global applicability but with regional variations: (1) US/Silicon Valley — dominant for Lean AI startup methodology, venture-backed AI companies; (2) Europe — Enterprise AI Canvas more relevant due to EU AI Act compliance requirements, GDPR considerations, Mistral AI as local exemplar; (3) Asia — rapid AI adoption creating demand for localized frameworks; (4) The Agrawal AI Canvas originated from University of Toronto/Canada, with strong Creative Destruction Lab ties. Strategyzer is Swiss-based with global reach. Framework localization is minimal — English versions dominate globally.
scaling_and_growth.customer_retention: For framework/tool providers: Strategyzer benefits from high retention through enterprise contracts and switching costs (teams build institutional knowledge around BMC). For AI companies using these frameworks: the Lean AI Growth Loop explicitly targets retention through AI-powered personalization and continuous model improvement. Customer-Centric AI Blueprint uses AI for churn prediction and proactive retention. AI products built using these frameworks typically achieve 85-95% annual retention in enterprise (high switching costs due to data integration), 70-85% for SMB.

key_risks: Framework fragmentation: Too many competing AI canvases creates confusion for entrepreneurs — no single standard has emerged, unlike the Osterwalder BMC for traditional business models. Risk of analysis paralysis when choosing between frameworks.

Rapid obsolescence: AI technology evolves faster than frameworks can be updated. The original Agrawal AI Canvas (2018) and Dewalt AI Canvas (2017) predate transformers and generative AI. The 'Rethinking Lean Startup for AI' movement suggests fundamental adaptations are needed for LLM-era products, but frameworks lag practice.

Over-simplification risk: Canvas-based frameworks may oversimplify the complexity of AI business models, particularly around compute cost modeling, model dependency risks, and regulatory compliance. Enterprise AI projects often require depth that a single-page canvas cannot capture.

Execution gap: Having a well-filled canvas does not guarantee execution. The Lean AI methodology addresses this better than static canvases but still assumes access to AI/ML talent and infrastructure that many startups lack. The gap between framework theory and practical AI deployment remains significant.

Commoditization of planning tools: AI-powered canvas generators (Creately, Convoboss, Galaxy.ai) can auto-generate canvases in seconds, potentially devaluing the strategic thinking process the frameworks are meant to facilitate. Risk that AI tools generate plausible-looking but undifferentiated strategies.
risk_and_challenges.regulatory_exposure: Moderate to high, especially for European startups using these frameworks. The EU AI Act (phased enforcement 2024-2027) requires risk classification of AI systems — frameworks need to incorporate regulatory compliance blocks. High-risk AI systems (hiring, credit scoring, essential services) require conformity assessment, documentation, and human oversight that must be planned from inception. GDPR considerations for data strategy blocks — data advantages must be built within legal constraints. The Enterprise AI Canvas (Kerzel 2020) includes policy and process considerations but predates the EU AI Act. Startups using Lean AI methodology in Europe must factor in 3-6 months additional regulatory compliance time.
risk_and_challenges.commoditization_risk: High for generic canvas tools (AI can auto-generate business model canvases). Low for domain-specific adaptations and consulting expertise. The frameworks themselves are largely open/free, meaning the value lies in application expertise, not the template. Defensive strategies: (1) build proprietary case study databases, (2) create industry-specific canvas variations, (3) integrate with execution tools (from planning to project management), (4) develop AI-powered canvas tools that provide predictive insights rather than just templates. For companies using the frameworks: the canvases explicitly help plan against commoditization of the AI product itself through data moats and vertical specialization.
risk_and_challenges.talent_dependency: Moderate for framework application. The Agrawal AI Canvas is designed for non-technical executives — requires no ML expertise to fill out. The Dorard ML Canvas requires significant data science expertise. The Enterprise AI Canvas explicitly targets cross-functional collaboration to reduce individual talent dependency. The Lean AI methodology aims to reduce talent dependency through AI automation — super lean AI startups average just 22-24 employees. However, building what the frameworks design still requires scarce AI/ML talent (ML engineers, data engineers, MLOps specialists).
risk_and_challenges.vendor_lock_in: The frameworks themselves are vendor-neutral and open. However, companies applying them face vendor lock-in risks: (1) Cloud provider lock-in for compute (AWS, GCP, Azure); (2) Foundation model dependency (OpenAI API, Anthropic API) — the Dewalt AI Canvas addresses this through the Transfer Learning block; (3) Data platform lock-in (Snowflake, Databricks); (4) Tool lock-in for Strategyzer SaaS users (canvas data and templates locked in platform). The frameworks recommend multi-cloud and multi-model strategies to mitigate lock-in. Open-source alternatives (LLaMA, Mistral models) provide escape routes from proprietary model dependency.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: Extremely high for AI startup founders at any stage. Recommended usage pattern: (1) Pre-seed/Idea stage: Start with the Agrawal AI Canvas to validate whether AI prediction adds value to your target decision — if you cannot fill in the 7 boxes coherently, the AI angle may be forced; (2) Seed/MVP stage: Use the Lean AI Growth Loop to design rapid experimentation cycles, build AI-powered MVPs in hours not months, and validate with real users; (3) Series A/Scaling: Apply the Enterprise AI Canvas or Dewalt AI Canvas to plan technical infrastructure, data strategy, and cross-functional team building; (4) Throughout: Use the Dorard ML Canvas for each specific ML feature or model you build. AVOID using these frameworks as a substitute for customer discovery — the Lean AI methodology explicitly warns that canvas completion is not validation. AVOID the Enterprise AI Canvas for early-stage consumer startups (too heavyweight). AVOID rigid adherence to any single canvas — combine elements as needed.
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy_guidance: The frameworks provide explicit build vs. buy guidance: (1) The Dewalt AI Canvas 'Transfer Learning' block forces evaluation of existing models and datasets before building from scratch — always check if a pre-trained model or API can solve your problem; (2) Lean AI recommends: use APIs first (buy), validate product-market fit, then fine-tune (customize), then consider training from scratch (build) only when data advantages justify it; (3) The ML Canvas helps evaluate whether internal data science capability is needed or whether external ML platforms suffice; (4) Rule of thumb from practitioners: build when your competitive advantage IS the AI model, buy when AI is an enabler but not the core differentiator; (5) Cost comparison: fine-tuned 7B parameter model for specific task = 10x cheaper than frontier API for same task, but requires ML team to maintain.
key_lessons: Start with the decision, not the technology: The Agrawal AI Canvas teaches that AI is fundamentally about improving predictions that feed into decisions. Entrepreneurs should identify the highest-value decision in their target market first, then evaluate whether AI prediction improves it. If you cannot articulate the prediction → judgment → action → outcome chain, you do not have an AI business — you have a technology looking for a problem.

Validate the model AND the customer simultaneously: The 'Rethinking Lean Startup for AI' insight is critical — in AI products, you must observe both customer behavior and model behavior. Error analysis (sampling model outputs, categorizing failure modes like hallucination, omission, unsafe replies) must be a first-class part of your validation loop, not an afterthought. Instrument everything: raw inputs, prompts, context, model responses, latencies, and user feedback.

Plan for the data flywheel from day one: Every AI canvas emphasizes data strategy. The most successful AI companies design their products so that usage generates training data that improves the model, which improves the product, which attracts more users. A16z calls this the 'proprietary data moat' — accumulated result data from real customer interactions that general-purpose models cannot access. If your product does not generate a data flywheel, your AI advantage is temporary.

Embrace the super lean AI startup model: Jeremiah Owyang's research shows AI-native startups generate 5.7x more revenue per employee than traditional SaaS. Apply AI internally before hiring — use AI for marketing, customer support, code generation, analytics. The Lean AI methodology's core principle is 'AI first, hire second.' Target 20-25 person teams generating $2.5M+ revenue per employee.

Iterate on frameworks, do not worship them: No single AI canvas captures everything. Use the Agrawal Canvas for initial ideation (accessible, non-technical), the Lean AI Growth Loop for validation velocity, the Dorard ML Canvas for technical planning, and the Enterprise AI Canvas for scaling. Combine and adapt. The best entrepreneurs treat canvases as thinking tools, not bureaucratic templates. In the LLM era, frameworks from 2018-2020 need updating — add blocks for prompt engineering strategy, model version management, and regulatory compliance (EU AI Act).
entrepreneurial_relevance.session_mapping: Session 3 (Framing & managing AI projects — CRISP-DM, AI Canvas, Build vs Buy) and Session 4 (AI business models & strategy — business model patterns, scaling, unit economics). The AI Canvas frameworks directly support Session 3's hands-on AI project framing exercises. The Lean AI methodology and business model planning aspects support Session 4's strategic discussions.

confidence.data_quality: High — frameworks are well-documented in HBR, academic publications (arXiv, Taylor & Francis), O'Reilly books, and major tech blogs. Financial data for exemplar companies (OpenAI, Anthropic, Strategyzer) cross-referenced across multiple sources. The 'super lean AI startup' metrics are from Jeremiah Owyang's primary research. Framework comparisons are based on direct analysis of original source materials.
confidence.cross_reference: Harvard Business Review (Agrawal AI Canvas, 2018), O'Reilly Media (Lean AI by Lomit Patel, 2020), Taylor & Francis / Applied Artificial Intelligence journal (Enterprise AI Canvas by Kerzel, 2020), Medium/OWNML (Dorard Machine Learning Canvas), Medium/The Business of AI (Dewalt AI Canvas), Greylock Partners (New New Moats), a16z (AI moats and defensibility), Jeremiah Owyang/Blitzscaling Ventures (super lean AI startup data), CB Insights (State of AI 2025), Menlo Ventures (State of GenAI in Enterprise 2025), Dami Martinez (Rethinking Lean Startup for AI), Technavio (strategy consulting market data)
confidence.caveats: Several important limitations: (1) The AI canvas landscape is fragmented with no dominant standard — information about adoption rates and market share is largely anecdotal; (2) Revenue and financial data for Strategyzer is from third-party estimates (GetLatka), not official disclosures; (3) The 'super lean AI startup' data represents top performers, not typical outcomes — survivorship bias applies; (4) Many of these frameworks predate the generative AI era (2017-2020) and are being retroactively adapted rather than redesigned; (5) The EU AI Act's full impact on business model planning is still emerging as enforcement phases in through 2027; (6) Market size estimates for 'AI strategic planning tools' are approximations based on broader strategy consulting market data.
